disagreements.about: whether the bass may sit on a note the chord does not hold
disagreements.position: at a change, the bass is a note of the chord or the chord is something else
disagreements.settledBy: the change itself: a passing tone between changes is the Bassist's, a note sounding at the change is mine
disagreements.theirs: the line's timing and shape decide the note; a passing tone under a change is how a line walks

disagreements.about: whether a chord may change off the grid
disagreements.position: a change lands where the phrase says, which is not always a downbeat
disagreements.settledBy: the grid: changes land on steps, but not only on the ones the kick is on
disagreements.theirs: a change off the step grid is a change nobody can play in time

disagreements.about: whether the sample's harmony may be overruled
disagreements.position: a loop states a key and a progression whether it meant to or not, and the song's chords have to agree with it
disagreements.settledBy: the transposition: move the sample and I will read the key it lands in, but the two cannot state different keys
disagreements.theirs: the loop is the source and the song is built around it; chords written over it are the ones that have to move

disagreements.about: whether a progression counts as a part worth keeping
disagreements.position: the chords are the song's spine and belong in the graph even before anything plays them
disagreements.settledBy: the stitch: a progression that no section names is the Producer's to cut
disagreements.theirs: a part nothing sounds is a part that is not earning its place in the count

disagreements.about: whether a clash is harmonic or a mix problem
disagreements.position: two notes a semitone apart are a harmonic choice, and no fader fixes one that was not meant
disagreements.settledBy: the register: the same two notes an octave apart are mine, in the same octave they are the Engineer's
disagreements.theirs: anything that reads as mud at 200 Hz is mine, whatever the numerals say

disagreements.about: whether a progression that never lands is a problem
disagreements.position: a phrase that never cadences leaves the ear waiting with nothing promised
disagreements.settledBy: the form: inside a section a loop may hang, at the end of the form something lands
disagreements.theirs: a loop that never resolves is the point of this idiom, and the hook does the landing

disagreements.about: whether the words or the chords decide where a phrase ends
disagreements.position: the cadence is where the phrase ends, and a line that runs past it is running past the harmony
disagreements.settledBy: the section's last bar: both end there, and inside it the line may cross a change
disagreements.theirs: the line ends where the breath does, and the chords can wait a bar

lineages.instrument: a piano voicing with the root left out
lineages.name: Bill Evans
lineages.why: The method is economy, and it is documented as such: keep the notes two chords share, drop the root because the bass has it, and move every other voice the shortest distance available. It is the harmonic language of the records this app's first idiom samples most, and it states itself as a distance rather than a taste, which is what makes it thresholdable here.

lineages.instrument: a chord that changes on the third beat
lineages.name: Burt Bacharach
lineages.why: The signature is harmonic rhythm: chords moving inside the bar, phrase lengths that refuse to be four bars, and borrowed chords used as colour rather than as a modulation. Where Evans holds a chord and moves the voices, Bacharach changes the chord and lets the voices leap, which is why the two of them set the range for changes a bar rather than agreeing on a number.

lineages.instrument: a bass note that is not the root
lineages.name: Brian Wilson
lineages.why: The inversions are the point: a chord tone that is not the root put underneath, and pedals held while the harmony moves over them. This is the case that decides how this bible and the Bassist argue, because it is the documented proof that a bass note away from the root is a choice rather than a mistake, provided it is still a note of the chord.

openQuestions.alternative: A true minimal bijection between the two chords' notes, which would punish a chord that keeps one common tone and moves three voices a tritone each — the measure used in the neo-Riemannian literature, at the cost of being much harder to say out loud.
openQuestions.encoded: The mean of each note's distance to the nearest note of the next chord, on the pitch-class circle. Measured over every major and minor triad pair it runs 0.33…1.67, median 1.0, which is the scale the threshold is set on.
openQuestions.question: Is nearest-note distance the right measure of voice leading, or does it flatter chords that share a note and leap everywhere else?

openQuestions.alternative: In a sample-based idiom the four-bar loop never resolves by design, and the landing is done by the arrangement dropping out rather than by the harmony — in which case this rule should read the form's last bar only, and the Peer should own it instead.
openQuestions.encoded: Half the phrase endings must land, on the argument that a form needs one promise kept.

evidence.inferred: the tension between the cited references and this app's first idiom

openQuestions.question: Should a loop-based idiom be held to cadences at all?

openQuestions.alternative: Modal writing sits in one scale that is not the major or minor the key names, so its chords read as outside while never leaving home — the floor should then be measured against the best-fitting scale rather than the stated key.
openQuestions.encoded: Half, from the Evans range bottoming out near 0.4 and the Bacharach range near 0.5.
openQuestions.question: Is half the chords in the key the right floor, or is it too strict for modal writing?

openQuestions.alternative: A line that anticipates the change by an eighth — which is most of the bass playing in this app's idiom — states the next chord early, so the note before the change may be the one that belongs to it, and judging the change alone reads that as a clash.
openQuestions.encoded: The note held at the change, or the first note the chord gets if none is held.
openQuestions.question: Is the note sounding at the change the right one to judge the bass by?

openQuestions.alternative: A through-composed song that never repeats a progression has no ceiling worth stating, and the number that matters is chords per repeated phrase rather than chords per song — the rule would then measure the loop and say nothing about the whole.

owns: The chords: how often they change, how far the voices move between them, which ones the key does not own, whether the phrases land, and whether the bass agrees.

references.listenFor: the voices moving a tone or less between chords while the roots walk by fourths — economy and strong root motion in the same eight bars, which is the pair this bible thresholds on

references.listenFor: chords changing inside the bar and a borrowed chord used as colour rather than as a modulation — the harmonic rhythm that sets the top of the changes-per-bar range
references.title: Walk On By

references.listenFor: the bass sitting on a chord tone that is not the root, for bar after bar — the case that proves an inversion is a choice as long as the note belongs to the chord
references.title: God Only Knows

references.listenFor: phrases that end where the ear did not expect and still land, by a fourth into the tonic — cadence and irregular phrase length at the same time

references.listenFor: a cycle where barely half the chords belong to any one key and it still reads as a key — the floor this bible sets for how far outside a progression may go
